content: The Deacon process was a secondary chemical process employed during the production of alkalis, specifically sodium carbonate, as part of the Leblanc process. In this process, hydrogen chloride gas was oxidized to produce chlorine gas. The chlorine gas was subsequently utilized in the manufacture of commercially valuable bleaching powder. This innovation not only provided a useful product but also significantly reduced the emission of waste hydrogen chloride, which was a byproduct of the Leblanc process. The Deacon process represented a technically advanced improvement over the earlier manganese dioxide process. It was invented by Henry Deacon in 1874. The chemical reaction central to this process occurred at a temperature range of approximately 400 to 450°C in the presence of a copper chloride (CuCl₂) catalyst. Over time, the Deacon process became obsolete, as more efficient electrolytic methods for chlorine production were developed. However, recent advancements in catalysis, particularly with ruthenium(IV) oxide-based catalysts, have been explored. These developments were spearheaded by Sumitomo, and the first detailed mechanistic study of this new approach was published in the Journal of Catalysis, volume 255, page 29, in 2008. The Leblanc-Deacon process was a modification of the original Leblanc process, which was notorious for its severe environmental impact, contributing to some of the earliest air and water pollution legislation. In response to the Alkali Act of 1863, which mandated the reduction of harmful emissions, Henry Deacon devised a method to oxidize hydrogen chloride using oxygen over a copper chloride catalyst, producing chlorine gas. This chlorine was widely used in the paper and textile industries as a bleaching agent. As a result of this innovation, the production of sodium carbonate, which was the primary product of Leblanc process plants, became secondary. Consequently, sodium carbonate was often sold at a financial loss, as the focus shifted to the more commercially valuable chlorine and its derivatives.
